chapters.name: Chapter 1: What AI is and where you meet it

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI is, in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in two sentences what AI is and what it is not.
This lesson builds toward: In your own words, you will explain what AI is, how it learns from examples, and why it can be wrong, in two sentences a younger student can follow.
AI stands for artificial intelligence. It means computer programs that do things that usually need a person's thinking, like recognizing a face, understanding speech, suggesting a song or writing an answer.
Most AI learns from huge amounts of examples. A program that has seen millions of cat photos can guess whether a new photo has a cat in it. A program that has read huge amounts of writing can write sentences that sound like a person.
AI is not alive, it does not have feelings, and it does not truly understand the world the way you do. It finds patterns and makes its best guess. That is why it can be very useful and still be wrong.
Words to know:
- AI: artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need human thinking.
- Pattern: something that repeats in a way a program can learn and use to guess.
Try it now: Write two sentences that explain AI to a ten-year-old. Use no word they would not know. Read it to someone and ask if it made sense.
You can now explain what AI is and what it is not in two plain sentences.

check.q: What does it mean that AI "finds patterns"?
options: It knows everything about the world
It learns from many examples and makes its best guess
check.why: AI learns from huge numbers of examples and guesses based on the patterns it found.

check.q: Your friend says, "AI is alive and understands me." What do you tell them?
options: AI is not alive and has no feelings; it guesses from patterns
Yes, it has feelings like a person
check.why: AI is a program that finds patterns; it is not alive and does not truly understand.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Spotting AI in the apps you already use
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name at least three places AI shows up in your everyday apps.
This lesson builds toward: Using the apps on your phone or a school computer, you will identify where AI suggests, sorts, guesses or creates something, including generative AI, naming at least three apps and what the AI does in each.
You probably use AI every day without calling it that. Music and video apps suggest what to play next based on what you liked before. That is AI looking for patterns in your choices.
Phone cameras use AI to sharpen photos and blur backgrounds. Keyboards guess your next word. Maps guess traffic. Games use AI to control characters you play against. Email and messaging apps filter spam.
Chat assistants, such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini, are a newer kind called generative AI. Instead of only sorting or suggesting, they make new text, pictures or sound.
Step by step:
- Open an app you use a lot.
- Ask: is it suggesting, sorting, guessing or creating something for me?
- If yes, that is probably AI at work.
- Write the app name and what the AI does.
Words to know:
- Recommendation: a suggestion an app makes based on what you did before.
- Generative AI: AI that makes new things, such as text, images or music.
Try it now: Go through the apps on your phone or a school computer. List three that use AI and write one line for each saying what the AI does, for example "Music app: suggests songs I might like".
You can now spot AI in everyday apps and say what it is doing.

check.q: What makes generative AI different from a music app's song suggestions?
options: It makes new text, pictures or sound
check.why: Generative AI creates new content instead of only sorting or suggesting.

check.q: You want to know if an app uses AI. Which question helps most?
options: Is it suggesting, sorting, guessing or creating something for me?
check.why: If an app suggests, sorts, guesses or creates for you, AI is probably at work.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Age limits, school rules and your parent or guardian
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check whether you may use an AI tool, at home and at school, before you sign up.
This lesson builds toward: Before you use a new AI tool at home or at school, you will check the tool's age rule and your school's AI rules, and show the app to a parent or guardian, using the tool's official help or terms page.
Every AI tool has rules about who can use it. Many need you to be at least 13, and some ask for a parent or guardian's permission if you are under 18. Google, for example, says you must be 13 or over (or the age that applies in your country) to use Gemini with a personal or school account. Rules change, so read the tool's own terms or help page.
Your school has rules too. Some classes allow AI for brainstorming but not for writing your work. Some ban it for tests. Using it against the rules can count as cheating, even if you did not mean it to. When in doubt, ask your teacher before you use it.
Before you make an account on any new app, talk with a parent or guardian. Show them the app, its age rule and what information it asks for. Many schools also give you a school account for approved tools; use that one for schoolwork.
Step by step:
- Find the tool's age rule on its official help or terms page.
- Check your school's and your teacher's AI rules.
- Show a parent or guardian the app before you sign up.
- Use your school account for approved school tools.
Words to know:
- Terms of use: the rules a company sets for using its app or website.
- Academic integrity: being honest about your schoolwork: the work you hand in shows what you did.
Official sources:
- Google Gemini Apps Help: what you need to sign in (age requirement)
Try it now: Pick one AI assistant. Find its age rule on the company's own help or terms page. Then write down your school's or one teacher's rule about AI. Show both to a parent or guardian.
You can now check an AI tool's age rule and your school's AI rules, and involve a parent or guardian before signing up.

check.q: Where is the best place to find an AI tool's age rule?
options: The tool's own help or terms page
check.why: Rules change, so read them on the company's own help or terms page.

check.q: You are not sure if AI is allowed for a class project. What do you do?
options: Use it and hope it is fine
Ask a friend in another school
Use it but do not tell anyone
Ask your teacher before you use it
check.why: School rules differ, and using AI against them can count as cheating, so ask first.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using an AI assistant the smart way

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Asking a clear question
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear prompt that gets a useful answer the first time.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you want to learn, you will write a prompt that says what you want, some background and how you want the answer, so the first answer is useful.
What you type to an AI assistant is called a prompt. Clear prompts get better answers.
A good prompt has three parts: what you want, a bit of background, and how you want the answer. For example: "I am in 9th grade and we are starting a unit on the water cycle. Explain it in 5 short steps with one everyday example."
A weak prompt like "water cycle" makes the assistant guess what you need. You will usually get a long, general answer.
Step by step:
- Say what you want.
- Add a bit of background (your grade, the topic, what you already know).
- Say how you want it: steps, a list, short, simple words or an example.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant.
Try it now: Pick something you are curious about, like how a game engine works or why the sky is blue. Write a prompt with all three parts, send it to an AI assistant you are allowed to use, and read the answer.
You can now write a clear three-part prompt.

check.q: What is the "background" part of a prompt?
options: A bit about you and the topic, like your grade or what you already know
check.why: Background, like your grade and topic, helps the assistant fit the answer to you.

check.q: You typed "volcanoes" and got a long, general answer. What do you send next?
options: "I am in 8th grade. Explain how volcanoes erupt in 4 short steps."
check.why: Adding what you want, background and the format makes the prompt clear.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking the answer before you trust it
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI answer against at least one trusted source.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer with facts in it, you will check names, dates and numbers against a trusted source, noting where you checked each fact.
AI assistants sometimes make things up. They can invent a date, a quote, a book that does not exist, or a fact that sounds right but is wrong. This is called a hallucination.
Check anything important, especially facts for school, health, money and news. Look in your textbook, ask your teacher or librarian, or find a trusted site, such as a museum, a science agency, an encyclopedia your school uses, or a site ending in .gov or .edu.
A good habit: compare two sources. If the AI and a trusted source disagree, trust the source, and maybe tell your teacher what the AI got wrong.
Step by step:
- Find the facts in the answer: names, dates, numbers.
- Look up each one in a trusted source.
- If they disagree, go with the trusted source.
- Note where you checked.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Source: where information comes from.
Try it now: Take the answer from your last prompt. Pick two facts in it and check each one in a trusted source. Write down whether each was right and where you checked.
You can now spot facts that need checking and check them in a trusted source.

check.q: Which is a trusted source for checking a school fact?
options: Your textbook or a site ending in .edu or .gov
check.why: Textbooks, teachers, librarians and trusted sites are good places to check facts.

check.q: The AI names a book for your report, but you cannot find it anywhere. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a possible hallucination and use a source you can find
Put it in your report anyway
Ask the AI to promise it is real
check.why: AI can invent books and facts; trust sources you can actually check.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying safe and being fair with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI without sharing private information and without hurting anyone.
This lesson builds toward: When you write a prompt or see AI-made content, you will keep private information out, refuse to make fakes of real people, and question unfair answers, sharing no private details and telling a trusted adult about hurtful fakes.
Do not type private information into an AI tool: your full name with your address, your school and schedule, phone numbers, passwords, or photos of friends without asking. What you type may be saved.
AI can make fake pictures, fake voices and fake videos, sometimes called deepfakes. Never use AI to make fake or embarrassing pictures of real people. It can hurt them, break school rules and even break the law. If someone does it to you or a friend, tell a trusted adult.
AI can also be unfair. It learned from human writing, so it can repeat stereotypes. If an answer seems unfair to a group of people, question it.
Step by step:
- Read your prompt before you send it and remove private details.
- Never make fake images or voices of real people.
- If you see a hurtful deepfake, tell a trusted adult.
- Question answers that seem unfair.
Words to know:
- Deepfake: a fake picture, voice or video made with AI to look real.
- Bias: when a result is unfair to some people, often because of what the AI learned from.
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page "AI explainer": what AI is in two sentences, three apps you use that have AI, and one question you asked an AI assistant with the answer and how you checked it. Make sure it has no private information in it.
You can now use AI safely and fairly, and explain AI to someone else.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds What AI is The explanation is missing, wrong or too hard for a younger student. Two clear sentences that say what AI is and that it can be wrong. Also says how AI learns from examples, in words a ten-year-old would know. AI in my apps Fewer than three apps, or no line on what the AI does. Three apps, each with one line on what the AI does. Also points out which one is generative AI. Clear question The prompt is one or two words. The prompt says what you want, some background and how you want the answer. The answer was useful the first time, or one follow-up made it better. Answer checked The answer was used without checking. At least one fact checked in a trusted source, and the source is named. Two facts checked in two sources, with a note on anything the AI got wrong. Safe and allowed The explainer has private details, or the tool was used against its age rule or school rules. No private information, and the tool used fits its age rule and school rules. Adds a tip for the younger reader about staying safe with AI. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why keep private information out of AI tools?
options: What you type may be saved
check.why: What you type may be saved, so private details like your address and schedule stay out.

check.q: A friend wants to use AI to make a funny fake picture of a classmate. What do you do?
options: Help make it but do not share it
Post it, since it is a joke
Say no, because fakes of real people can hurt them and break rules
Send it only to close friends
check.why: Fake pictures of real people can hurt them, break school rules and even break the law.
